newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish Riksbank sees recovery, cuts rates again.
newsitem.headline: Swedish Riksbank sees recovery, cuts rates again.

text.p: Sweden's Riksbank on Tuesday signalled its growing faith in the country's nascent economic recovery in an upbeat inflation report that coincided with the 20th cut this year in the bank's key interest rate.
In its latest quarterly report on economic developments and and monetary policy, the central bank said inflation in Sweden -- now running at just 0.6 percent -- had been held firmly in check.
"The prospect of inflation during 1997, as well as in the first half of 1998, being in line with the two percent inflation target is good," the bank said.
In fact, inflation had been lower than envisaged in the bank's last report, which was published in June.

"This is primarily because the transitory effects of falling interest rates and import prices have been greater than expected," the Riksbank said, adding that economic developments had otherwise been in line with its previous assessments.
With the threat of inflation firmly banished, the central bank said way was clear for further cuts in its key interest rate, the repo rate.

This was underlined just half an hour after the publication of the inflation report as the bank trimmed the repo rate, which is its main monetary policy tool, by a further 10 basis points to 5.05 percent in what was the 20th such move this year.
The repo rate has fallen by almost four percentage points from 8.91 percent in January, whilst the crown has steadily appreciated against the mark and the rate of inflation has continually fallen.
The main cloud on the Swedish economic horizon has been growth, or lack of it, but the Riksbank said it was slightly more optimistic in this respect too.
"The economic slowdown towards the end of 1995 was brief, and there has been an upturn during 1996," the bank said.
"A total growth rate of three to four percent for 1996 and 1997 combined is still considered most probably, although today the emphasis is in the upper half of this interval."

What could upset the inflationary apple cart is wage-driven price rises. The annual rate of wage increases in the second quarter of the year was 6.2 percent, which was 1.1 percentage points higher than in the first quarter.

Deputy Riksbank governor Lars Heikensten told Reuters Financial Television that although wages were the greatest threat to the Riksbank's inflation scenario, he did not believe the effects would be dramatic.
"I am not too worried for the next year or two primarily because we don't think that demand wil be strong enough to leave room for prices to go up," Heikensten said.
"But in a longer perspective the wages increases we have had here during 1996 are clearly too high."
Analysts said that although the Riksbank would be keeping a close check on consumer demand, any wage-led rise in inflation would be modest.

"CPI inflation proper would be via a pickup in consumer demand, but our best guess is that this will remain sluggish so I'm looking for moderate upturn," analyst Katharina Hoyland of JP Morgan told Reuters.

With almost four hundred basis points of repo rate cuts yet to filter through to the economy, (four percentage points) the Riksbank is likely to take a "breather" to reassess the situation when the repo rate dips below five percent, she said.
"Our current forecast is for the rate to bottom out at around 4.75 percent, but I wouldn't rule out that they can go further than that. After all, real interest rates are still high," Hoyland said.
